# Galaxy Types {#sec-galaxy-types}

*"The cosmic menagerie"*

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Revelation
Galaxies come in distinct types, but these are not fixed categories: they represent different evolutionary states, shaped by mergers, environment, and star formation history.
:::

## The Hubble Classification

### Hubble's Tuning Fork

![The Hubble tuning fork classification: ellipticals on the left, lenticulars at the junction, and spirals branching into normal and barred types on the right.](../../media/images/fig-hubble-fork.png){#fig-hubble-fork}

This is NOT an evolutionary sequence, but rather a classification scheme based on morphology.

## Elliptical Galaxies (E)

Smooth, featureless spheroids.

### Properties

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Shape | Spheroidal to elongated |
| Stars | Old, red |
| Gas | Very little |
| Star formation | None (dead) |
| Population | ~15% of galaxies |

### Classification

E0 to E7 based on apparent ellipticity:
- E0: Circular
- E7: Most elongated

### Examples
- M87 (giant elliptical in Virgo)
- NGC 1132 (fossil group)

## Spiral Galaxies (S)

Disk galaxies with spiral arms.

### Structure

![Spiral galaxy structure showing the disk with spiral arms, central bulge, and surrounding dark matter halo.](../../media/images/fig-spiral-structure.png){#fig-spiral-structure}

Spiral galaxies consist of a thin rotating disk containing spiral arms, a central bulge of older stars, and an extended spherical halo containing old stars, globular clusters, and dark matter.

### Properties

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Structure | Disk + bulge + halo |
| Stars | Mix of old and young |
| Gas | Significant in disk |
| Star formation | In spiral arms |
| Population | ~70% of bright galaxies |

### Subtypes

| Type | Bulge | Arms | Gas |
|------|-------|------|-----|
| Sa | Large | Tight | Less |
| Sb | Medium | Moderate | Medium |
| Sc | Small | Open | More |
| Sd | Tiny | Very open | Most |

### Barred Spirals (SB)

Central bar connects to spiral arms:
- Possibly a phase, not permanent
- Affects gas flow
- Milky Way is SBbc

## Lenticular Galaxies (S0)

Intermediate between elliptical and spiral.

### Properties
- Disk but no arms
- Little gas or star formation
- Old stellar population
- Possibly "faded" spirals

## Irregular Galaxies (Irr)

No regular structure.

### Types
- **Irr I**: Some structure visible
- **Irr II**: Chaotic, often interacting

### Examples
- Large/Small Magellanic Clouds
- Many dwarf galaxies

## Galaxy Properties

| Type | Mass | Diameter | Example |
|------|------|----------|---------|
| Giant elliptical | $10^{13}$ $M_\odot$ | 300 kpc | M87 |
| Large spiral | $10^{11}$ $M_\odot$ | 30 kpc | Milky Way |
| Dwarf elliptical | $10^7$ $M_\odot$ | 1 kpc | Many |
| Dwarf irregular | $10^8$ $M_\odot$ | 3 kpc | SMC |

## Why Different Types?

### Formation History
- Gas-rich mergers → spirals
- Gas-poor mergers → ellipticals

### Environment
- Clusters → more ellipticals
- Field → more spirals

### Transformation
Spirals can become ellipticals through:
- Major mergers
- Ram pressure stripping
- Strangulation (cut off from gas)

## The Morphology-Density Relation

![The morphology-density relation: elliptical galaxies dominate in dense cluster environments, while spirals are more common in the field.](../../media/images/fig-morphology-density-relation.png){#fig-morph-density}

Dense environments such as galaxy cluster centers are dominated by elliptical and lenticular galaxies, while spiral and irregular galaxies are more common in lower-density field environments.

### Environment Effect

## Concepts

- **elliptical**: Smooth, spheroidal, old stars
- **spiral**: Disk with arms, ongoing star formation
- **lenticular**: Disk without arms
- **irregular**: No clear structure

## Transition

The Milky Way is our home galaxy: a barred spiral. We now explore our cosmic neighborhood in detail.
